abstract_before: Dealers monitor the largest absolute position reached before a review horizon ends. We compare conditional quantile models with historical rules using hourly FX positions, weekly New York Fed positions and dealer aggregates in 17 CFTC futures markets. Histories and update schedules are matched. Historical rules are hard to beat. First, FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% across two periods, but its ranking against a shorter rolling rule changes. Second, historical rules beat regression in 34 of 48 New York Fed comparisons and 29 of 34 CFTC comparisons; finite-penalty hindsight still favors history in most short weekly comparisons. They usually remain in the model confidence set alongside alternatives. In calibrated simulations, expanding the penalty menu cuts the constant-parameter median excess loss from 116.2\% to near zero; switching adds no observed median loss in this short-history comparison. Third, in CFTC, lower scores need not mean lower limit costs: higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor expanded regression. The evidence is retrospective, and the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.

contributions_before:
The paper makes three empirical findings.

\textit{First, matched FX gains recur, but rankings against a shorter rolling rule change.} The period comparisons separate conditioning gains from the reference procedure (Table~\ref{tab:fx}). Delayed calibration preserves the later matched gain while changing breach behavior. Within the original FX period, the full-regression learning curve improves at intermediate histories but gives back part of the gain at the longest history (Figure~\ref{fig:v11-history}).

\textit{Second, historical rules remain competitive in weekly data, where both penalty selection and the finite menu leave losses.} The panel and independent CFTC reporting system favor historical controls in most comparisons, and historical methods usually survive joint forecast comparison (Table~\ref{tab:weekly} and Supplement Table~\vthirteenMCSTable{}). Even the best finite penalty chosen with evaluation hindsight loses in 29 of 41 short-history weekly comparisons (Section~\ref{sec:v12-low-frequency}). Longer validation narrows CFTC losses and selects the intercept-only limit more often, linking tuning instability to the available validation history. Expanded simulation menus also bring short-history regression near its historical reference, with no additional observed median loss from parameter switching. These retrospective diagnostics distinguish a finite-menu gap from selection errors, without ruling out other conditional signals.

\textit{Third, higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor expanded regression in CFTC.} The direction has local exceptions (Figure~\ref{fig:v10-cost}). Lower scores therefore need not mean lower limit costs, and validation should report reserve amounts, breach counts and exceedance amounts together.
contributions_after:
The paper makes three empirical findings.

\textit{First, matched FX gains recur across periods but remain reference-dependent.} Long-history regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\%, while its ranking against the shorter rolling rule changes (Table~\ref{tab:fx}). The original-period learning curve improves with more history before surrendering part of the gain at the longest history (Figure~\ref{fig:v11-history}). Matching peak responses, completed labels and refit schedules makes these comparisons interpretable without isolating causal feature effects.

\textit{Second, longer validation improves weekly regression medians while leaving large individual-task losses.} Historical controls remain competitive in both weekly reporting systems, while extended validation reduces regression medians (Table~\ref{tab:v13-validation}). The CFTC short-history median excess falls from 19.3\% to 4.0\%, and New York Fed medians also improve. A benchmark-default protocol retains FX gains and has zero weekly median excess, but 8 of 60 cases still lose by over ten percent (Section~\ref{sec:v13-rp}). These are retrospective arm-median comparisons; the horizon-six New York Fed extension also moves the validation boundary.

\textit{Third, lower scores leave limit-cost rankings sensitive to prices.} Expanded regression is cheaper in 5/34 CFTC cases at the grid center, and in 32/34 or 1/34 at opposite corners (Figure~\ref{fig:v10-cost}). Higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor regression, with local exceptions. These illustrative preferences motivate joint reporting of reserves, breaches and exceedance amounts, while institutional costs remain unmeasured.

conclusion_before:
Historical rules are hard to beat. For RQ1, matched FX regression gains recur across periods, but the shorter rolling reference changes the ranking and history gains are not monotone. Delayed calibration preserves the later matched gain with a small breach-count difference, reinforcing the need to interpret conditioning gains under explicit histories and update schedules.

For RQ2, historical controls remain competitive across related weekly aggregates and same-record daily FX, usually surviving joint comparison alongside alternatives. The finite-penalty hindsight diagnostic leaves losses in most short weekly comparisons, while longer validation improves CFTC selection toward historical reports. Both menu limits and selection errors therefore matter within the tested procedures; neither result rules out every possible conditional signal. Expanded simulation menus bring short-history regression near its historical reference, with switching adding no further observed median loss in that comparison. Numerical failures prevent a complete assessment at the higher quantile level, leaving the original gains without a demonstrated extension there.

For RQ3, higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor expanded regression in CFTC, with local exceptions. Lower forecast scores therefore need not imply lower limit costs. Validation should report reserve amounts, breach counts and exceedance amounts together, using the cost regions in Figure~\ref{fig:v10-cost}.
conclusion_after:
Historical rules are hard to beat. For RQ1, matched FX regression gains recur across periods, but a shorter rolling reference changes the ranking (Table~\ref{tab:fx}). The learning curve also gives back part of its gain at the longest history, linking conditional performance to available history rather than universal model advantage (Figure~\ref{fig:v11-history}).

For RQ2, longer validation reduces full-regression medians in both weekly reporting systems, but across-arm differences need not describe typical paired improvements (Table~\ref{tab:v13-validation}). These dealer aggregates remain related tasks, and the horizon-six New York Fed extension also moves the validation endpoint. The benchmark-default protocol cuts weekly median excess to 0.00\% and preserves FX gains, yet 8 of 60 cases still lose by over ten percent, including a worst 80.98\% (Section~\ref{sec:v13-rp}). This failed tail criterion limits the protocol's risk-management recommendation, and the rejected high-quantile repair leaves its original judgments unresolved.

For RQ3, higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor expanded regression in CFTC, with local exceptions (Figure~\ref{fig:v10-cost}). Lower pinball scores can therefore coexist with more breaches and different cost rankings, requiring joint reporting of reserve amounts, breach counts and exceedance amounts. The costs are stipulated preferences rather than observed institutional costs, and the financial evidence remains retrospective.
practical_before: \textbf{Use historical headroom by default when validation evidence is short.} Expanded penalties and longer validation reduce losses, but short-sample selection, including one-standard-error selection, still fails to protect the historical benchmark consistently. Historical reports also survive in most CFTC model confidence sets, supporting their retention until a conditional procedure has sufficient validation evidence. The ordinary empirical quantile is up to 36.5\% worse than corrected headroom in the earlier weekly grid.
practical_after: \textbf{Use historical headroom by default when validation evidence is short.} Longer validation and a paired standard-error gate improve the weekly median, but leave eight large losses in the complete comparison (Section~\ref{sec:v13-rp}). Passing this gate alone therefore fails to establish adequate benchmark protection. The ordinary empirical quantile is up to 36.5\% worse than corrected headroom in the earlier weekly grid, supporting a separately validated historical default.
